title: OOP internals
scopeHtml: Scope: object memory layout, vtables and dispatch, constructor order, equals/hashCode contract, immutability and defensive copies.

notes.title: What an object is in memory
notes.html:
An object is a block of bytes on the heap; a variable holds a reference (an address-like handle) to it. Copying a reference copies the handle, not the object. This one fact explains aliasing bugs, == vs equals, and defensive copies.

On HotSpot (64-bit) an object has a header then fields:

  • Mark word: 8 bytes (hash code, GC age, lock state).
  • Class pointer: 4 bytes with compressed oops (default for heaps under about 32 GB), else 8.
  • Fields, aligned; total size rounded up to a multiple of 8.
class Point { int x; int y; }

offset  size  content
0       8     mark word
8       4     class pointer (compressed)
12      4     x
16      4     y
20      4     padding -> total 24 bytes

Worked example. One million Point objects = 24 MB of objects plus the array of references (4 MB with compressed oops) = 28 MB. A primitive int[] pair (int[] xs, ys) holds the same data in 8 MB. This is why games and Android code avoid millions of tiny objects (GC pressure, cache misses).

Industry examples. Android's SparseArray and IntArray avoid boxing; Kotlin value class and Java's Project Valhalla (value types, in progress; confirm status for your JDK) aim to remove headers. Tools: JOL (Java Object Layout) prints real layouts.

Everyday analogy. A variable is a sticky note with a locker number. Copying the note gives two notes for one locker.

Common interview traps.

  • "Java passes objects by reference." It passes references by value; reassigning the parameter does not change the caller's variable.
  • Forgetting boxing: an Integer is about 16 bytes versus a 4-byte int.
  • == compares references, not contents.

notes.title: Virtual dispatch and vtables
notes.html:
When you call a.speak() and a might be a Dog or Cat, the JVM picks the method at runtime. That is dynamic dispatch (polymorphism).

Mechanism: each class has a vtable, an array of method pointers. A subclass copies its parent's table and replaces overridden slots. a.speak() becomes "load class pointer, index slot k, jump". Cost: one extra indirection. HotSpot's JIT usually removes it: if only one class is loaded for a call site it inlines (monomorphic); with two it checks type (bimorphic); beyond that it uses the vtable (megamorphic, slower, no inlining).

Animal vtable:  [0]=Animal.speak  [1]=Animal.eat
Dog vtable:     [0]=Dog.speak     [1]=Animal.eat     (overrides slot 0)
Animal a = new Dog();
a.speak();       // dispatched on the runtime class (Dog)
open class Animal { open fun speak() = "..." }
class Dog : Animal() { override fun speak() = "Woof" }

What is NOT virtual. static, private, final methods and constructors are bound at compile time. Fields are never polymorphic: they use the declared type ("field hiding"). Kotlin classes and members are final by default; Java's are open by default.

Worked example. static call: 0 dispatch cost. Monomorphic virtual call: about 0 after inlining. A megamorphic interface call over 5 implementations in a hot loop may cost 3 to 5 ns extra per call; for 100M calls that is 0.3 to 0.5 s.

Industry examples. Android ART does devirtualization too. Kotlin's final default and sealed classes help the compiler. interface calls use itables (slightly slower than class vtables in older JVMs).

Everyday analogy. A phone book per department: you look up "speak" in the Dog's own book.

Common interview traps.

  • Overloading is resolved at compile time on the declared types; overriding at runtime.
  • Calling an overridable method from a constructor (next section).
  • Thinking private methods can be overridden; they cannot.

notes.title: Constructor order and initialization
notes.html:
Java builds an object parent first, then child. For new Child():

  1. Memory is allocated and zeroed (all fields default 0/null/false).
  2. Child() starts and calls super(...) first (explicitly or implicitly).
  3. The parent runs its field initializers and instance blocks, then its constructor body.
  4. Then the child's field initializers and instance blocks, then the child constructor body.

Static initializers run once per class at class initialization, parent first, before any instance.

class Parent {
    Parent() { System.out.println("Parent ctor"); init(); }
    void init() { System.out.println("Parent init"); }
}
class Child extends Parent {
    private String name = "child";
    Child() { System.out.println("Child ctor, name=" + name); }
    @Override void init() { System.out.println("Child init, name=" + name); }
}
// new Child() prints:
// Parent ctor
// Child init, name=null     <- field not yet assigned!
// Child ctor, name=child
open class Parent { init { println("Parent init"); hook() }; open fun hook() {} }
class Child : Parent() {
    private val name = "child"
    override fun hook() { println("name=$name") }   // prints name=null
}

Worked example. The bug: an overridden method called from the parent constructor sees null or 0 in child fields; a NullPointerException at startup that "works in tests with a mock". Cost to debug: hours.

Rule. Never call overridable methods from a constructor. Make it final/private, or use a factory or a separate init() called after construction.

Industry examples. Android View constructors calling overridable onFinishInflate-like hooks; frameworks like Spring use @PostConstruct precisely to run after full construction.

Everyday analogy. You must pour the foundation before the walls: the parent builds its part before the child exists.

Common interview traps.

  • Predicting output order; practise this exact snippet.
  • this(...) and super(...) must be the first statement (relaxed in newer Java previews; confirm version).
  • Kotlin lateinit / property initialization order in the primary constructor.

notes.title: equals and hashCode contract
notes.html:
If you override equals, you must override hashCode. HashMap and HashSet find an object by hashCode first (picks the bucket), then equals (confirms). Break the pair and lookups silently fail.

The equals contract: reflexive (x.equals(x)), symmetric, transitive, consistent over time, and x.equals(null) is false. The hashCode contract: equal objects must have equal hash codes; unequal objects may share a hash (collisions) but should spread out.

final class Money {
    private final long cents; private final String currency;
    Money(long c, String cur) { cents = c; currency = cur; }
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
        if (this == o) return true;
        if (!(o instanceof Money m)) return false;
        return cents == m.cents && currency.equals(m.currency);
    }
    @Override public int hashCode() { return java.util.Objects.hash(cents, currency); }
}
data class Money(val cents: Long, val currency: String)   // equals/hashCode/toString generated

Worked example. A User with equals on id but no hashCode: set.add(u1); set.contains(new User(sameId)) returns false 15 of 16 times (default identity hash lands in another bucket of a 16-bucket table). Intermittent, hence nasty.

Pitfalls. Mutable fields in hashCode: mutate a key after inserting it and the entry becomes unreachable (a leak). Inheritance and equals with instanceof breaks symmetry (Point vs ColorPoint); prefer final classes or composition. Avoid floating == in equals (use Double.compare). JPA entities: equality on a generated id that is null before save is a known trap.

Industry examples. Effective Java (Bloch) items 10 and 11; Lombok @EqualsAndHashCode; Kotlin data classes; Guava Objects. Java 8 HashMap converts long buckets (8+ entries) to trees, so bad hashes cost O(log n) instead of O(n) but still hurt.

Everyday analogy. The hash is the building and floor; equals is checking the apartment's name plate. Wrong building, you never find them.

Common interview traps.

  • Overriding one but not the other.
  • Using mutable fields as hash keys.
  • equals(Foo f) instead of equals(Object o): that is an overload, not an override. @Override catches it.

notes.title: Immutability
notes.html:
An immutable object never changes after construction. Safe to share between threads without locks, safe as a map key, and easy to reason about.

Recipe: final class (or private constructor), all fields private final, no setters, no leaking mutable internals (copy in, copy out), do not let this escape from the constructor.

public final class Event {
    private final String name; private final Instant at; private final List<String> tags;
    public Event(String name, Instant at, List<String> tags) {
        this.name = name; this.at = at;
        this.tags = List.copyOf(tags);          // defensive copy, also immutable
    }
    public List<String> tags() { return tags; }  // safe: already unmodifiable
    public Event withName(String n) { return new Event(n, at, tags); }   // "wither"
}
data class Event(val name: String, val at: Instant, val tags: List<String>)
val e2 = e1.copy(name = "new")    // copy instead of mutate

Worked example. String is immutable, so its hash is cached; a 1 M entry HashMap<String,...> computes each hash once. Sharing one Config across 200 threads needs zero locks. Cost: each "change" allocates a new object (e.g. building a string in a loop of 100,000 with + is O(n squared); use StringBuilder).

Industry examples. String, Integer, java.time, BigDecimal, Kotlin val and read-only collections, Redux-style UI state, Compose state, immutable messages in Kafka.

Decision gravity. Starting immutable is cheap; making a mutable class immutable later breaks every setter caller (one-way door). Mutable is justified for hot paths and builders.

Everyday analogy. A printed receipt: to change it, you issue a new receipt.

Common interview traps.

  • final on a field does not make the object immutable; the list inside can still change.
  • Kotlin List is a read-only view, not necessarily immutable; the backing MutableList may still change.
  • Forgetting to make the class final so a subclass adds mutability.

notes.title: Defensive copies
notes.html:
A defensive copy is a private duplicate you make so outside code cannot change your internals. Needed at two points: when you receive a mutable argument and when you return a mutable field.

class Booking {
    private final Date start;                       // Date is mutable (legacy)
    Booking(Date start) { this.start = new Date(start.getTime()); }   // copy in
    Date start() { return new Date(start.getTime()); }               // copy out
}
// Without copies: Date d = new Date(); Booking b = new Booking(d); d.setTime(0);  // corrupts b!
class Roster(players: List<String>) {
    private val players = players.toList()          // copy in
    fun all(): List<String> = players.toList()      // copy out (or expose read-only view)
}

Worked example. A Cart returns its internal ArrayList of 100 items. A UI bug calls .clear() on it; the cart silently empties. Copying costs 100 pointer copies (about 0.3 microseconds), negligible against the bug.

Cheaper options. Collections.unmodifiableList(list) is a view (no copy, but changes to the backing list show through); List.copyOf makes a real immutable copy (no copy if already immutable); use immutable types (java.time) and you need no copies.

Shallow vs deep. Copying a list copies references; if elements are mutable, the elements are still shared. Copy elements too, or make them immutable.

Industry examples. JDK's Arrays.asList is a fixed-size view over the array (writes pass through); Android Bundle/Intent extras and Parcelable copy across processes.

Everyday analogy. You give a friend a photocopy of your key list, not the original keys.

Common interview traps.

  • Copying in the getter but not in the constructor (or vice versa).
  • Shallow copy of nested mutable objects.
  • Performance panic: copies are usually cheap; measure first.
  • clone(): widely discouraged; prefer copy constructors or factories.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• An object = header (mark word 8 B, class pointer 4 B) + fields, padded to 8 B; variables hold references, passed by value.
  • Virtual calls use vtables; static/private/final are bound at compile time; JIT inlines monomorphic sites.
  • Construction order: zeroed memory, parent init and ctor, child init and ctor; never call overridable methods in a constructor.
  • Override equals and hashCode together; use immutable fields in the hash; mind the equals(Object) signature.
  • Immutability: final class, final private fields, no setters, copy mutable inputs/outputs; Kotlin val and read-only List are not deep immutability.
  • Defensive copies at the boundary (copy in, copy out); prefer immutable types to avoid them.

questions.promptHtml: Is Java pass-by-reference or pass-by-value for objects? What actually lives in a variable that "holds" an object?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who memorised "objects are by reference" from those who know a variable holds a handle and the handle is copied.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Java is always pass-by-value. For objects, the value copied is the reference, a handle to the heap object. So the callee can mutate the object through its copy of the handle, but reassigning the parameter does not change the caller's variable.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A local variable of class type is a slot on the stack (or in a field) containing a reference. new Point() allocates a block on the heap: 8-byte mark word, 4-byte compressed class pointer, then fields, padded to a multiple of 8. A Point{int x,y} is 24 bytes.

caller: p ---> [Point x=1 y=2]
callee: q ---^      (q is a COPY of p's handle)
q = new Point()  -> q now points elsewhere, p unchanged
q.x = 9          -> both p and q see x=9 (same object)

== compares handles; equals compares content (if overridden).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
static void mutate(Point q) { q.x = 9; }          // visible to caller
static void reassign(Point q) { q = new Point(); } // invisible to caller

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "objects pass by reference"; a swap(a, b) method cannot work in Java.
  • == on String/Integer (interning and the Integer cache make it work "sometimes").
  • Forgetting that Integer is about 16 bytes versus 4 for int.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can you write a working swap(Object a, Object b)? -> No; only by wrapping in a holder or array.
  2. What does final Point p guarantee? -> The handle never changes, not that the object is unchanged.
  3. How would you check the real object size? -> JOL (Java Object Layout) prints header, fields and padding.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer stops at "by value of the reference". The senior ties it to aliasing bugs, defensive copies, header cost and GC pressure for millions of small objects.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A shared mutable config object passed into a worker "for reading" was mutated by the callee; every other holder of the handle saw the change.

questions.promptHtml: Animal a = new Dog(); a.speak(); How does the JVM decide which speak to run?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether "polymorphism" is understood as a mechanism and not only a word.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Each class has a vtable, an array of method pointers. The call loads the object's class pointer, indexes the slot for speak, and jumps. Dog copied Animal's table and replaced the overridden slot, so the runtime class decides, not the declared type.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Animal vtable:  [0]=Animal.speak  [1]=Animal.eat
Dog vtable:     [0]=Dog.speak     [1]=Animal.eat
a.speak() => load a.klass -> vtable[0] -> call

Cost is one extra indirection. HotSpot's JIT profiles each call site: one receiver class seen (monomorphic) means inline it with a cheap type guard; two (bimorphic) inline both; more (megamorphic) falls back to the vtable or itable with no inlining. Interface calls use itables, historically a bit slower.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
open class Animal { open fun speak() = "..." }
class Dog : Animal() { override fun speak() = "Woof" }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking dispatch is decided by the declared type of the variable.
  • Saying virtual calls are "slow"; monomorphic ones usually cost nothing after inlining.
  • Believing private methods can be overridden.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which calls are NOT dispatched dynamically? -> static, private, final, constructors, and super.m().
  2. What is a megamorphic call site? -> One with 3+ receiver types, so the JIT cannot inline.
  3. How does Kotlin differ by default? -> Classes and members are final unless marked open, which helps devirtualization.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "runtime picks the method". Senior: vtable slots, JIT inline caches, monomorphic/bimorphic/megamorphic, and the cost model.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Hot paths with plug-in interfaces had inlining defeated after a third implementation was loaded.

questions.promptHtml: Why must you override hashCode whenever you override equals?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A classic fundamentals check with real production consequences in hash collections.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: HashMap and HashSet use hashCode to choose a bucket and then equals to confirm. If two equal objects have different hashes they land in different buckets, so contains and get silently miss. The rule: equal objects must have equal hash codes.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
equals must be reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent, and false for null. hashCode must be stable while the fields it uses are unchanged, equal for equal objects, and well spread for unequal ones (collisions allowed, but they cost time: a bucket with 8+ entries becomes a tree, O(log n)).

key -> hashCode -> bucket 7 -> equals(candidate) -> value

Default Object.hashCode is identity-based, so two equal-by-content objects almost never share it.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
    if (this == o) return true;
    if (!(o instanceof Money m)) return false;
    return cents == m.cents && currency.equals(m.currency);
}
@Override public int hashCode() { return java.util.Objects.hash(cents, currency); }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• equals(Foo f) instead of equals(Object o): an overload, not an override. Use @Override.
  • Using mutable fields in hashCode.
  • Overriding only one of the two.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is hashCode allowed to return a constant? -> Legal, but O(n) or O(log n) lookups.
  2. How does Kotlin help? -> data class generates both from primary-constructor properties.
  3. What about double fields? -> Compare with Double.compare, not ==, to handle NaN and -0.0.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "needed for HashMap". Senior: bucket mechanics, tree bins, mutable-key leaks, inheritance symmetry, JPA id traps.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A dedupe Set<User> let duplicates through intermittently because hashCode was missing.

questions.contextHtml:
A settings screen base class and a subclass are shipped. In staging it crashes at startup with an NPE; in unit tests with a mocked subclass it passes.

abstract class Panel {
    Panel() { System.out.println("Panel ctor"); render(); }
    abstract void render();
}
class TitlePanel extends Panel {
    private final String title = "Settings";
    private final StringBuilder out = new StringBuilder();
    TitlePanel() { System.out.println("TitlePanel ctor"); }
    @Override void render() { out.append(title.toUpperCase()); }
}
Panel ctor
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "java.lang.StringBuilder.append" because "this.out" is null
    at TitlePanel.render(TitlePanel.java:6)
    at Panel.<init>(Panel.java:3)

The team suspects the title constant, the JDK version, and a missing @Override.
questions.promptHtml: Why does it crash, and how do you fix it without changing the public API?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Initialize out in render" or "add a null check". That hides the symptom and the design stays fragile (note title happens to work because a final String initialised with a literal is a compile-time constant and is inlined; a non-constant initializer would also be null here).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is render ever overridden elsewhere? Do subclasses add more state? Is the object created via DI or new? Which Java version (field/ctor rules differ for records and previews)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Guard the crash with a lazy-init flag only if a hotfix is needed; ship a proper fix next.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) overridable call in a parent constructor sees unassigned child fields; (b) JDK difference (no, order is fixed by the JLS); (c) missing @Override (not relevant, it is present).
  4. How I'd verify each: Print order with a debugger breakpoint in render; observe this.out == null. Order is: zeroed memory, Panel field init, Panel ctor body (calls render), then TitlePanel field init, then TitlePanel ctor body.
  5. Root cause: The child's initializers have not run when the parent constructor calls the overridable render; fields hold default values.
  6. Fix: Short-term: move the call out of the constructor. Long-term: factory that constructs then calls render().
abstract class Panel {
    final void init() { render(); }          // called by factory after construction
    abstract void render();
}
static TitlePanel create() { var p = new TitlePanel(); p.init(); return p; }
  1. Prevention: Static analysis rule (Sonar S1699: constructors should not call overridable methods), code review checklist, make the hook final/private.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not sprinkle null checks; that encodes the bug into the contract. A two-phase init has its own risk (forgetting init()), so hide it behind a factory.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if title were static final String? -> A compile-time constant is inlined, so it would work; non-constants would not.
  • Kotlin equivalent? -> An init {} block calling an open fun has the same issue; properties initialize in declaration order.
  • Does @PostConstruct fix it? -> Yes, it runs after the full construction.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An Android custom view called an overridable hook from its constructor; a subclass property was still null, only on a cold start path. Moving the hook to onFinishInflate ended the crash.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds null checks without explaining order.
  • Hire: states the init order and moves the call out.
  • Strong hire: also gives the factory/post-construct pattern, lint rule, and constant-inlining nuance.

questions.promptHtml: What makes a class truly immutable in Java? Is a class with only final fields immutable?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks understanding of shallow versus deep immutability and of publication safety.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Final class, private final fields, no setters, and no leaking of mutable internals (copy in, copy out). final fields alone are not enough: a final List field can still be mutated, and a non-final class lets a subclass add mutability.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• final fixes the reference, not the referent.
  • Safe publication: final fields get a happens-before guarantee at the end of the constructor (JMM), so other threads see fully built state without locks, provided this does not escape during construction.
  • Benefits: free thread-safety, stable map keys, cacheable hash (String).
  • Cost: every change allocates (a loop doing s += x 100,000 times is O(n squared)); use a builder for assembly.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
public final class Event {
    private final List<String> tags;
    public Event(List<String> tags) { this.tags = List.copyOf(tags); }
    public List<String> tags() { return tags; }
}
data class Event(val tags: List<String>)   // read-only view, NOT deeply immutable

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking Kotlin val or read-only List is immutable; the backing MutableList may be modified by its owner.
  • Leaving the class non-final.
  • Letting this escape (registering a listener) in the constructor.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. unmodifiableList vs List.copyOf? -> View over a live list versus a real immutable copy.
  2. Why is String immutable? -> Caching hash, string pool, security (class names, paths), thread safety.
  3. Is it a one-way door? -> Yes; making a mutable type immutable later breaks every setter caller.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average lists the recipe. Senior adds JMM final-field semantics, this escape, the copy-cost trade-off and one-way-door thinking.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An "immutable" config exposing its Map caused cross-thread corruption when one component edited it.

questions.contextHtml:
A dedupe job collects User records into a HashSet<User> to skip already-processed users. Most duplicates pass through (testers saw it as intermittent), so a customer gets two welcome emails. Fully reproducible only with large input.

class User {
    final long id; final String email;
    User(long id, String email) { this.id = id; this.email = email; }
    public boolean equals(User o) { return o != null && id == o.id; }
}
// seen.add(u1); seen.contains(new User(1, "a@x.com"))  -> sometimes true, mostly false

Red herrings: "the set is not thread-safe" (it is single-threaded), "Java 21 regression".
questions.promptHtml: Find all bugs and explain why it is only intermittent.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add hashCode." Misses that equals(User) is an overload, so even with hashCode the set would call Object.equals (identity) and still fail every time.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the set shared across threads? Is id the true identity or is email? Any inheritance of User?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add an idempotency guard (unique key in the DB for the email send) so duplicates cannot reach customers.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) equals(User) is an overload; (b) no hashCode; (c) mutable fields in the hash; (d) thread safety (ruled out).
  4. How I'd verify each: @Override on equals fails to compile; unit test new User(1,..).equals((Object) new User(1,..)) is false; print hashCode() of equal users to see different identity hashes.
  5. Root cause: HashSet calls equals(Object), which is still the identity-based Object version, and hashCode is identity-based too. A new instance with the same id almost never hits the same bucket, and even if it does, equals(Object) says false. So a logical duplicate is missed nearly always; tests that re-query the same instance pass, which makes it look intermittent.
  6. Fix:
@Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
    return this == o || (o instanceof User u && id == u.id);
}
@Override public int hashCode() { return Long.hashCode(id); }
  1. Prevention: Always @Override; use records/data classes; Error Prone EqualsHashCode and EqualsUnusedHashCode checks; contract tests with EqualsVerifier.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not hash email if it can change; I would not just return a constant hash to "make it work".

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Does a Kotlin data class fix it? -> Yes, but only for primary-constructor properties.
  • Would final class matter? -> Yes, it avoids instanceof symmetry issues in subclasses.
  • Why did the original report say "1 in 16"? -> It was a misleading estimate; with identity hashes a duplicate is missed almost always, only the same instance is found.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A campaign system sent duplicate coupons because a value class had only equals; EqualsVerifier in CI caught seven more classes with the same flaw.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: only says "add hashCode".
  • Hire: finds overload and missing hashCode.
  • Strong hire: explains why tests passed, adds EqualsVerifier and idempotency guard.

questions.contextHtml:
A shopping Cart exposes its items. A UI bug clears the displayed list and the cart silently empties. A fix attempt wraps the getter in Collections.unmodifiableList, but a nightly report still sees items change mid-iteration (ConcurrentModificationException, 3 times in 1,000 runs).

class Cart {
    private final List<Item> items = new ArrayList<>();
    Cart(List<Item> initial) { items.addAll(initial); }
    List<Item> items() { return Collections.unmodifiableList(items); }
    void add(Item i) { items.add(i); }
}
// report thread: for (Item i : cart.items()) total += i.price();

Red herring: "ArrayList is slow".
questions.promptHtml: What remains wrong, and what is the right API shape?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "unmodifiableList is a copy." It is a live view; changes to the backing list show through.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Size of the cart (100 items?) and read frequency? Is Item mutable? Multi-threaded access?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Return List.copyOf(items) from the getter now.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) view not copy, report iterates while add runs; (b) Item mutable, so elements are shared; (c) constructor kept the caller's list (not here, addAll copies).
  4. How I'd verify each: Stress test with two threads; check Item for setters; heap dump not needed.
  5. Root cause: Unmodifiable view prevents the caller from writing but not the owner; iteration races with add.
  6. Fix: Return a snapshot; or make the cart immutable with a wither.
List<Item> items() { return List.copyOf(items); }  // 100 refs, about 0.3 microseconds
Cart with(Item i) { var n = new ArrayList<>(items); n.add(i); return new Cart(n); }

Make Item immutable (shallow copy shares elements). 7. Prevention: Review rule "never return a mutable field"; tests that mutate the returned list; ImmutableList types. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not locking the list for the reader (couples threads). Copying costs little; measure before avoiding it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Cart of 2M items read per request? -> Expose an iterator or immutable persistent structure, not a copy per call.
  • Kotlin List return? -> Still the same object; call .toList().
  • Arrays.asList input? -> Fixed-size view over the array; writes pass through, copy it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "read-only" list handed to an analytics module was cleared by a cleanup hook; orders vanished for 40 minutes before a snapshot copy was added.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: believes the wrapper is a copy.
  • Hire: snapshot copy and shallow-copy caveat.
  • Strong hire: immutable design, cost reasoning for large collections, tests.

questions.contextHtml:
A map-tile service keeps 20 million Point(int x, int y) objects in an ArrayList<Point>. Heap is 4 GB, GC logs show young pauses of 80 ms and old-gen at 85% after warm-up. Product wants 3x more points next quarter.

[GC pause (G1 Evacuation) 3071M->2890M(4096M) 84.2ms
jcmd GC.class_histogram:  Point 20,000,000 instances  480,000,000 bytes
                          Object[] ... 80,000,000 bytes

Red herrings: "switch GC to ZGC", "give the box more RAM".
questions.promptHtml: Explain where the memory goes and how you would cut it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase heap or tune GC." Does not reduce the data; at 3x the same problem returns.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are points mutated? Is access sequential or random? Do we need identity per point? Is the order stable?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Raise heap modestly if the pager is firing; no more.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) 24 B per object plus 4 B reference is 28 B for 8 B of data; (b) pointer chasing wrecks cache locality; (c) GC copying cost grows with live objects.
  4. How I'd verify each: class histogram (above), JOL to confirm 24 B layout (12 B header, 8 B data, 4 B padding), a quick JMH loop comparing both layouts.
  5. Root cause: 12 B header + padding is 50% overhead per object, and every object is a separate heap node the GC must trace.
  6. Fix: Short-term: store two int[] (or one interleaved int[2n]), 8 B per point: 160 MB instead of 560 MB. Long-term: a small PointStore class exposing x(i), y(i).
final class PointStore {
    private final int[] xs, ys;
    PointStore(int n) { xs = new int[n]; ys = new int[n]; }
    int x(int i) { return xs[i]; }
    int y(int i) { return ys[i]; }
}
  1. Prevention: Heap histograms in the perf runbook, capacity model per entity, alert on live-set growth.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not do this prematurely; the struct-of-arrays code is less readable. I would wait for Valhalla value types only after verifying status for the JDK in use.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Android context? -> IntArray, SparseIntArray, avoid boxing.
  • Need to sort points? -> Sort an index array or pack into a long (x << 32 | y).
  • Compressed oops off (heap over about 32 GB)? -> Header and refs grow, so waste grows.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A geo-indexing service dropped from 14 GB to 3 GB by moving from objects to primitive arrays; GC pauses fell from 200 ms to under 20 ms.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tunes GC or buys RAM.
  • Hire: computes object overhead and uses primitive arrays.
  • Strong hire: includes locality, tradeoff in readability, and verification with JOL/JMH.

questions.promptHtml: Which parts of a Java class hierarchy are bound at compile time rather than dispatched at runtime, and why does that matter?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Overloading versus overriding and field hiding are favourite trick questions, and they cause real bugs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Static, private and final methods, constructors, and fields are not virtual. Overloads are chosen at compile time from the declared argument types. Only overridable instance methods dispatch on the runtime class.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Parent p = new Child();
p.name        -> Parent.name   (field: declared type)
p.staticM()   -> Parent.staticM (hidden, not overridden)
p.m()         -> Child.m       (virtual)
print(Object) vs print(String) with Object x = "hi" -> print(Object)

Overload resolution is a compile-time lookup on static types; overriding is a runtime lookup on the receiver's class. Kotlin makes this safer by defaulting classes and members to final.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class A { String name = "A"; String who() { return "A"; } }
class B extends A { String name = "B"; @Override String who() { return "B"; } }
A a = new B();
System.out.println(a.name + a.who());   // prints AB

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming field access is polymorphic.
  • Thinking a static method can be overridden (it is hidden).
  • Expecting print(Object x) to pick String overloads at runtime.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a private method be overridden? -> No; a same-named subclass method is a new method.
  2. Is super.m() virtual? -> No, it is bound to the parent implementation (invokespecial).
  3. Why do final classes help the JIT? -> No subclasses possible, so calls devirtualize without guards.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average lists static/final. Senior distinguishes bytecode (invokevirtual, invokespecial, invokestatic, invokeinterface) and connects it to API design (final by default).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A subclass "overrode" a private helper to change behaviour; nothing happened and the bug stayed for months.

questions.contextHtml:
A session cache Map<SessionKey, Session> grows from 200 MB to 3 GB over a week and then OOMs. Lookups for a fraction of active sessions return null, so users are re-authenticated. Heap dump shows 4.1 million SessionKey entries; business says there are 90k active sessions.

class SessionKey {
    String userId; String device;           // device changes on re-login
    @Override public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(userId, device); }
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { /* userId + device */ }
}
// on device change: key.device = newDevice;  // key is already in the map
cache.get(key) -> null

Red herrings: "the TTL eviction is broken", "Caffeine bug".
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose the leak and the missing lookups, and fix it safely.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase TTL or heap." Misses that the entries are unreachable by key, so no eviction path finds them.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Who mutates keys and when? Is the map a plain HashMap or a cache with a TTL? Are entries ever removed by key? How are keys created?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restart rolling nodes; add a periodic full rebuild of the map by iterating entrySet() (iteration still finds them).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) key mutated after insertion; (b) eviction removes by key hash and misses; (c) unbounded key creation; (d) actual session leak.
  4. How I'd verify each: Heap dump: group by userId to see duplicates; a debug assert re-hashing every key in a test; compare entry.getKey().hashCode() with the bucket index.
  5. Root cause: The entry sits in the bucket computed from the old hash. After mutation, get computes a new hash and looks elsewhere, so it is lost and also not removable by key: a leak.
  6. Fix: Immutable key (record), re-insert with a new key on device change.
record SessionKey(String userId, String device) {}
Session s = cache.remove(old); cache.put(new SessionKey(userId, newDevice), s);
  1. Prevention: Keys immutable by lint rule/code review; use records; test "mutate then lookup".
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not recompute buckets by hand or rehash the map; I would not keep device mutable "for convenience".

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why is the entry still iterable? -> Iteration walks buckets; only lookup uses the hash.
  • Could a TreeMap help? -> Same issue with comparison order.
  • What if the key must carry a changing field? -> Exclude it from equals/hashCode.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A routing table keyed on a mutable Endpoint object slowly lost 8% of routes after health-check updates; moving to a record key removed the pager noise.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: raises TTL/heap.
  • Hire: finds mutable key, makes it immutable.
  • Strong hire: explains bucket mechanics, why it leaks, and the safe migration.

questions.contextHtml:
A geometry library adds ColorPoint extends Point. A unit test in the checkout module intermittently fails depending on argument order.

class Point { final int x, y;
  @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
    if (!(o instanceof Point p)) return false;
    return x == p.x && y == p.y; } }
class ColorPoint extends Point { final String color;
  @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
    if (!(o instanceof ColorPoint c)) return false;
    return super.equals(o) && color.equals(c.color); } }
Point p = new Point(1, 2); ColorPoint cp = new ColorPoint(1, 2, "red");
p.equals(cp)  // true
cp.equals(p)  // false

Red herring: "make ColorPoint ignore color".
questions.promptHtml: What contract is violated, what are the options, and which would you choose?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Compare class with getClass()." That fixes symmetry but breaks Liskov substitution (a subclass instance no longer equals the base value where a Point is expected).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must a ColorPoint be usable as a Point? Is Point published for subclassing? What map/set usage exists?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revert ColorPoint's override or stop mixing the two in collections.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) symmetry broken by instanceof asymmetry; (b) transitivity trap if you "fix" it by letting ColorPoint compare to Point ignoring colour; (c) hashCode mismatch.
  4. How I'd verify each: EqualsVerifier fails with "Symmetry"; a small test of both directions.
  5. Root cause: There is no way to extend an instantiable class with a value component and preserve the equals contract (Effective Java, Item 10).
  6. Fix: Favour composition so ColorPoint has a Point and an accessor asPoint().
final class ColorPoint {
    private final Point point; private final String color;
    Point asPoint() { return point; }
    // equals compares point and color; no relationship to Point.equals
}
  1. Prevention: Make value classes final; records are final; use EqualsVerifier in CI.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: getClass() equality is legal but breaks LSP; "ignore colour" breaks transitivity (red(1,2) == p == blue(1,2) yet red != blue). I would choose composition.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Abstract base with no value state? -> Subclassing is fine; no conflict.
  • Kotlin? -> data class is final by default; cannot be open.
  • canEqual pattern? -> Works but is heavy; composition is simpler.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A domain Money and TaxedMoney subclass produced dedupe misses in a ledger only when sorted one way; a final record replaced both.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: cannot state the broken property.
  • Hire: names symmetry and proposes composition or final.
  • Strong hire: shows the transitivity trap and the LSP cost of getClass().

questions.promptHtml: How would you design equals and hashCode for a JPA entity with a database-generated id? Why is the naive version risky?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Real systems mix identity, value equality and lifecycle; this tests judgement more than syntax.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Never hash on a generated id that is null before persist, and never use all mutable fields. Either use a stable business key, or use identity-style equality with a constant hashCode per class. Do not use a Kotlin data class blindly for entities.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Problem sequence: entity created, id == null, added to a HashSet; saved, id assigned, hash changes, set loses it (mutable-key leak). Lazy proxies (Hibernate) subclass the entity, so getClass() equality fails and instanceof is required. A data class's generated equals touches all fields including lazy collections, triggering loads or recursion in bidirectional relations (StackOverflowError in toString/hashCode).

new Order() id=null -> set.add -> hash(null)
save()            id=42   -> hash(42) -> set.contains = false

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
    return this == o || (o instanceof Order other && id != null && id.equals(other.id));
}
@Override public int hashCode() { return getClass().hashCode(); }  // constant: stable across persist

Alternative: a natural key (e.g. orderNumber) assigned at construction.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Including relationship fields in hashCode.
  • getClass() != o.getClass() with proxies.
  • Using Lombok @Data or Kotlin data class on entities.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Constant hashCode, is that bad? -> It collapses collections of one type into one bucket; fine for small per-session sets, bad for 100k entities in a set.
  2. UUID assigned in the constructor? -> Best option: stable, unique before persist.
  3. Entity as map key across a persist boundary? -> Use the id value as the key, not the entity.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average writes Objects.hash(id). Senior walks through the lifecycle, proxies and chooses UUID/business keys, noting the constant-hash trade-off.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A set of line items "lost" members after save(), so totals double counted on retry.

questions.contextHtml:
A pricing RateTable is declared immutable ("final fields, no setters") and shared by 200 request threads. Occasionally, one request returns a price computed from half-updated rates (error rate 0.02%), and a reload thread throws ConcurrentModificationException once a day.

public final class RateTable {
    private final Map<String, Double> rates;
    public RateTable(Map<String, Double> src) { this.rates = src; }   // src is the loader's working map
    public Map<String, Double> rates() { return rates; }
    public double rate(String k) { return rates.get(k); }
}
// loader: working.put("EUR", 0.92); table = new RateTable(working);  // later working.put("EUR", 0.91)

Red herrings: "make rate() synchronized", "use volatile on table".
questions.promptHtml: The class is "immutable". Why does it misbehave, and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds synchronized everywhere; the object is still mutable via the leaked map and iteration still races.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Who owns working? How often does it reload (every 5 min)? How many entries (2,000)? Is the reference to the table swapped atomically?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Build a fresh map on each reload and hand it over once; stop reusing working.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) constructor stores the caller's mutable map (no defensive copy); (b) the getter leaks the map; (c) table field not safely published; (d) HashMap iteration during a put.
  4. How I'd verify each: Search for other holders of the same map (IDE "find usages"), a stress test mutating working while readers run, JMM reasoning: final fields are safely published only if the object is fully constructed and state does not change afterwards.
  5. Root cause: final protects the reference. Shared state is mutated by the loader and read concurrently by non-thread-safe HashMap.
  6. Fix:
public RateTable(Map<String, Double> src) { this.rates = Map.copyOf(src); }
// holder: private volatile RateTable current;  reload: current = new RateTable(fresh);
  1. Prevention: Immutability checklist in review, ImmutableMap/Map.copyOf, test that mutates the source after construction.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Copying 2,000 entries every 5 minutes is trivial. I would not add locks on every read; the copy-on-reload plus a volatile swap gives lock-free reads.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why volatile on the holder? -> To publish the new table reference with a happens-before edge.
  • Kotlin val rates: Map ? -> Read-only view; still copy in.
  • Entries 50M? -> Use a persistent/immutable structure or double-buffer arrays.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A feature-flag snapshot "immutable" by convention was rewritten in place by a debug endpoint; swapping to copy-on-write ended phantom flag flips.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds locks.
  • Hire: identifies the leaked mutable map and copies in.
  • Strong hire: adds volatile swap, publication semantics and test.

questions.contextHtml:
A rules engine evaluates Rule.apply(ctx) over 100 million events per run. When the fifth Rule implementation shipped, the batch time went from 38 s to 61 s. CPU profile shows the time inside Rule.apply stubs, not the rule bodies.

-XX:+PrintInlining
  @ 17 Engine::run (63 bytes)
     @ 22 Rule::apply (interface) virtual call   too many receiver types

Red herrings: "the new rule is slow" (it takes 40 ns), "GC".
questions.promptHtml: Why did adding one implementation slow the loop and what would you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Interface calls are slow, use abstract classes." Slightly true, but misses profile pollution and inlining.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Rule order in the list? How hot is each rule? Are the rules fixed at startup?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back or reorder so the loop runs per-rule type batches.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) call site became megamorphic and stopped inlining; (b) the new rule increased cache misses; (c) added allocation.
  4. How I'd verify each: -XX:+PrintInlining, JMH comparing 1, 2, 4, 5 implementations, async-profiler for cache-miss counters.
  5. Root cause: HotSpot inlines up to two receiver types per call site; with five it falls to an itable/vtable lookup with no inlining and no escape analysis through ctx.
  6. Fix: Short-term: group events/rules so each loop runs a monomorphic site; or switch on a sealed kind (devirtualized by hand). Long-term: batch API applyAll(List<Event>).
for (Rule r : rules) r.applyAll(events);   // each call site sees one receiver per loop
  1. Prevention: JMH benchmark in CI for hot paths; document the cost model.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not rewrite everything as switch, which hurts extensibility; measure first (5 ns x 100M is 0.5 s, this was 23 s so something else compounds).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Sealed types help? -> A hand switch can be devirtualized; the JIT may emit a type switch.
  • What about Graal? -> Often more aggressive inlining; verify for your runtime.
  • Is 23 s explained by dispatch alone? -> No; lost inlining also blocks escape analysis and vectorization.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A scoring pipeline slowed 30% after a plug-in was added; batching per implementation recovered it without changing the plug-in API.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames interfaces vaguely.
  • Hire: explains megamorphic inlining limits and re-structures the loop.
  • Strong hire: validates with PrintInlining/JMH and reasons about the 23 s gap.
